sections.html:
Louisa County is a rural county in central Virginia, about an hour's drive or less from Richmond, Fredericksburg and Charlottesville. The county seat is the town of Louisa, and the only other incorporated town is Mineral.

It covers 511 square miles, of which 496 are land and 15 are water. Neighbors are Orange, Spotsylvania, Hanover, Goochland, Fluvanna and Albemarle counties. In the 2020 census the Census Bureau classed every resident as rural.

That 14.7 percent vacancy figure is much higher than in nearby Hanover or Henrico counties. We do not have a sourced reason for it, so if you own an empty or seasonal house here, expect buyers and tax offices to ask about its status.

sections.h2: What is the history of Louisa County?
sections.html:
Louisa County was established in 1742 from Hanover County and named for Princess Louise of Great Britain, the youngest daughter of George II. Before colonial settlement the area was home to the Tutelo, Monacan and Manahoac peoples.

Patrick Henry lived here in the 1760s, and in 1765 he won his first election to the House of Burgesses to represent Louisa. The Virginia Central Railroad came through between 1838 and 1840, and it became a Confederate supply line, which led to cavalry fighting at Trevilians in 1864.

The twentieth century brought two unusual neighbors. Twin Oaks Community, one of the country's oldest secular communes, started in 1967, and Acorn Community followed in 1993. The Green Springs Historic District and Jerdone Castle are among the places the county's Wikipedia entry lists as points of interest.

sections.h2: How did Lake Anna and the 2011 earthquake change Louisa County?
sections.html:
Lake Anna, a 13,000-acre artificial lake, and the North Anna Nuclear Generating Station were built by Virginia Power in the 1970s. In recent years retirees settling near the lake and commuters have driven much of the county's growth, with at least fifteen new housing developments appearing in five years by 2008.

On August 23, 2011, a magnitude 5.8 earthquake struck Virginia, centered in Louisa County about five miles south-southwest of Mineral. Damage in the county topped $70 million.

  • $57.5 million to public school buildings
  • $11.5 million to residential structures
  • $400,000 each to religious and commercial buildings
  • $500,000 to government buildings

For sellers, the earthquake is a useful reminder that a buyer's inspector may ask about foundation cracks or chimney repairs on older houses. Keep any repair records and receipts together, and tell us honestly about past damage so our offer reflects the real condition.

sections.h2: Which communities and roads define Louisa County?
sections.html:
Besides Louisa and Mineral, the county has the census-designated place of Blue Ridge Shores and many unincorporated communities, including Apple Grove, Bumpass, Cuckoo, Ferncliff, Gum Spring, Holly Grove, Orchid, Trevilians, Yanceyville and Zion Crossroads.

Major highways are Interstate 64, U.S. 15, 33, 250 and 522, and State Routes 22, 208 and 231. A local Buckingham Branch freight train still passes the C&O depot and water tower in the town of Louisa. On a rural lot, check how water and sewage are handled and whether a community association applies, and gather those details before a sale.

Louisa County Public Schools serves the entire county as a single division.

sections.h2: How fast has Louisa County grown, and who lives here?
sections.html:
Louisa County had 20,325 residents in 1990, 25,627 in 2000, 33,153 in 2010 and 37,596 in 2020, then an estimated 42,924 in 2025. That is more than double in thirty-five years.

The 2020 census counted 14,921 households. About 27.7 percent had children under 18, 23.7 percent were one person living alone, and 20.5 percent of residents were 65 or older. With a fifth of residents 65 or older, estates and downsizing sales are part of the local picture.

Ask the office what documents the county wants if a personal representative signs for an estate. We have not confirmed those steps on an official county page.

sections.h2: What extensions can the county grant on real estate tax?
sections.html:
The county governing body may by resolution allow reasonable extensions of up to 90 days on real estate tax when good cause exists, and the official who grants one must keep a record. Members of the armed forces deployed outside the United States get an automatic extension on a primary residence until 90 days after deployment ends.

If omitted taxes are assessed, the locality may let the Treasurer set up a payment agreement of no more than 72 months, as long as current taxes are paid as they come due. Whether Louisa County has adopted these options is a question for the Treasurer.

sections.h2: Who handles real estate tax in Louisa County?
sections.html:
In Virginia, a county Treasurer bills and collects real estate tax, and the assessing office sets values. We could not open Louisa County's own tax pages for this guide, so we are not stating the county's tax rate, installment dates, penalty rates or appeal deadline. Please call the Treasurer's office and the county's real estate office to get them.

Ask for these items in writing:

  • Your current balance, with any penalty and interest broken out
  • The next due date and the last day to pay without penalty
  • The deadline and form for appealing an assessment
  • Whether the property is enrolled in any land use or relief program that could affect a sale

sections.h2: What Virginia protections apply to a late Louisa County tax payment?
sections.html:
State law limits what a county can do to a late payer, and Louisa County's ordinance has to stay inside those limits. A penalty for not paying real estate tax cannot exceed 10 percent of the tax past due, and interest cannot exceed 10 percent a year at first.

Several situations remove the penalty altogether:

  • The assessment was made less than two weeks before the due date through the fault of a local official, and it is paid within two weeks of the notice.
  • A payment arrives within five days by mail with a missing or unreadable postmark.
  • The taxpayer shows a Postal Service Certificate of Mailing or other proof of mailing from before the deadline.
  • The taxpayer died or had a medically determinable impairment on the due date, and payment follows within 30 days. A guardian or fiduciary gets 120 days after they begin to act.

Appeals also pause collection. A bill is not delinquent while an administrative appeal filed within 90 days of the assessment is pending, and for 30 days after the decision. The text is in Virginia Code 58.1-3916.

sections.h2: How does a Louisa County owner sell when taxes or repairs are a problem?
sections.html:
A Louisa County owner who is behind on tax, or who has inherited a house that needs work, can sell as is to a cash buyer and settle any tax balance at closing. An heir who takes over a property after a death also benefits from the fiduciary rule above, which gives a guardian or personal representative extra time after they qualify.

Cash Home Buyers can review a Louisa County house in any condition, including one near Lake Anna or on acreage, and provide a written cash offer. You are not obligated to accept, and you can ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure to compare with the offer.

faqs.q: Where is the Louisa County, Virginia tax office?
faqs.a: The county Treasurer collects real estate tax, but we could not confirm the office address or hours online. Contact the county directly to confirm.

faqs.q: How many people live in Louisa County?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 37,596 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 42,924.

faqs.q: What caused the 2011 earthquake damage in Louisa County?
faqs.a: A magnitude 5.8 earthquake on August 23, 2011, centered about five miles south-southwest of Mineral, caused more than $70 million in damage countywide.

faqs.q: Can a Louisa County tax penalty be waived after a death?
faqs.a: Virginia law presumes the taxpayer was not at fault if payment comes within 30 days of the due date after a death or medical impairment, and a fiduciary has 120 days after qualifying.
About 80.3 percent of occupied housing units were owner-occupied in the 2020 census, and 14.7 percent of all units were vacant.
